analysis.one_liner: Lets defrauded students cancel federal loans tied to misrepresentation by their school.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee after being referred there on the day it was introduced in July 2019, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When a college misrepresents its programs, its costs, or the employability of its graduates, this bill would have created a defense to repayment of the federal loans a student used to attend it, and would have required the Education Department to cancel the outstanding principal and interest and return payments already made. It broadened the bases for such a defense, including violations of state law, and required an expedited, fair process for individual and group claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Students defrauded by colleges, particularly those at for-profit institutions with strong recruitment claims and weak outcomes, who could have their federal loans canceled, outstanding interest waived, and payments refunded.

how_it_helps.text: It allowed a defense to repayment when an institution made a substantial misrepresentation of the nature of its educational program, its financial charges, or the employability of its graduates.

It allowed a defense to repayment for an act or omission by the institution that would give rise to a cause of action under applicable state law, or any other act or omission the Education Department specifies in regulation.
It required the Education Department, on finding a borrower entitled to relief, to cancel any outstanding principal and interest and to return any payments the borrower had made.

It required an expeditious and fair process for borrower defense applications, including applications submitted individually, by a group of borrowers, or by a representative, with decisions based on all available evidence.
It required that a determination on a borrower's claim be independent of any separate Education Department action to recover funds from the institution.

analysis.who_pays: Federal loan funds would be used to cover the cancellations and refunds, with the Education Department empowered to seek recovery from institutions whose misrepresentation caused the loss; institutions found to have defrauded students bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal loan funds and defrauding colleges

drawbacks.text: Cancellation and refunds would be paid out of federal loan funds up front, shifting costs to taxpayers until and unless the department successfully recovers from the institutions responsible.
The bill's final regulatory clause capped a borrower's recovery from the department at the amount already repaid on the loan, limiting the remedy for some borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to defrauded borrowers is significant, and the design attempts to hold responsible institutions accountable by making determinations independent of the department's recovery actions. The cost is the federal outlay for cancellations and refunds, which depends on how often relief is granted and how much the department recovers from institutions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor when introduced on July 10, 2019, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Lucy McBath (D-GA) introduced the Relief for Defrauded Students Act of 2019 in the House on July 10, 2019, with cosponsors including Finkenauer, Porter, Axne, Davids of Kansas, and Scanlon.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action on the bill; the recorded history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action during the rest of the 116th Congress.
The bill expired at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, without receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and institutions, particularly those facing borrower defense claims based on misrepresentation, were better off because the bill never advanced, as the statutory loan-relief pathway it would have created was never enacted.

for.name: Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: Finkenauer, Porter, Axne, Davids, and Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: No opposition is recorded in the action history, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown from the record.

industries.industry: Higher education institutions, especially for-profit colleges
industries.note: The bill would have allowed students to cancel federal loans based on a school's substantial misrepresentation or other violations, exposing institutions with predatory practices to large-scale debt cancellation and refunds. Schools that relied on misrepresenting programs, costs, or job prospects would have borne the cost.
